title: Korčula with a Dog 2027: Beaches, Ferries, Rules
metaDescription: Planning Korčula with a dog in 2027: dog beach Plitvine, old town, ferry rules, accommodation fees, heat, vets and EU pet passport requirements.
content:
## Are there dog beaches in Korčula?

The island has at least one named dog beach: **Plitvine in Vela Luka**, a fine-pebble beach on the western end of the island. Vela Luka is about 45 km from Korčula Town, so it suits a stay in the west more than a day trip from the old town. Several guides list up to six dog-bathing spots on the island, but the official status of most is unclear, so treat Plitvine as the only dependable one.

Croatia has no single national rule. Each municipality sets its own beach regulations, and many main town beaches restrict dogs in summer. Look for the signs at the entrance.

### Dogs on other beaches
Outside marked bathing zones, dogs are commonly seen on rocky and pebble coves around Korčula Town, Lumbarda (including the Tatinja area), and Pelješac across the channel near Orebić. The practical approach is to go early (before 9:00) or late (after 18:00), when beaches are nearly empty, and to keep the dog leashed near other swimmers. Avoid the sandy beaches of Lumbarda in peak hours. Sand beaches are the most strictly managed.

### Day trips with a dog
Badija island, a short boat ride from Korčula Town, has a walking trail around it. Keep dogs leashed and away from signed restricted beach areas. Proizd island has pebble beaches and one restaurant. Check the water taxi's dog policy before boarding, because operators set their own rules.

## Dogs in Korčula Old Town and restaurants
Leashed dogs are fine in the old town's lanes and on the waterfront promenade. The limestone paving gets very hot in July and August, so walk at dawn or after sunset. Stairs on the Korčula peninsula's herringbone street grid are steep, and small dogs may need carrying on crowded lanes.

Many konobas and cafés seat dogs on terraces, and the Dalmatian south region lists over 200 pet-friendly venues. Indoor dining rooms and food shops are typically off-limits. Ask before sitting down, since this is decided venue by venue.

## National parks and protected areas
Korčula has no national park. The nearest are Mljet National Park and Krka, and dogs are restricted or banned in parts of national parks, usually requiring a leash at all times. Check the park's rules before planning a day trip from Korčula. Inside the island, the Pelješac and Korčula forest paths are open for walks, but keep dogs leashed in summer for fire safety and wildlife.

## Ferries and catamarans with a dog
**Jadrolinija:** Local lines carry pets free of charge. Dogs must be leashed and muzzled, and they stay on the open deck. Larger dogs on catamarans (over 8 kg) travel in a reserved deck box, and the fee is quoted by the sales office on request. Small pets in a carrier up to 45x35x25 cm and 8 kg may sit in the catamaran lounge.

**Private catamarans:** Krilo's Split–Hvar–Korčula–Dubrovnik service charges 50% of the adult fare for a dog in a carrier and 100% for a dog in a deck cage. Adult fares are about €30 from Split and €25 from Dubrovnik, so a large dog can cost as much as a person. Some booking platforms show pets as not permitted on these routes, so confirm directly with the operator before paying.

**Car ferries are the easiest option.** The Orebić–Dominče crossing on Pelješac is short, and driving a dog onto a car ferry lets it stay in the vehicle or on deck with you. For a dog over 8 kg, a car ferry is more convenient than a catamaran in almost every case.

## Accommodation fees for dogs
Private apartments usually charge about €5–€20 per night, and some add a one-off cleaning fee. Hotels often charge more and may cap the number or size of dogs. Pets at hotels such as the 4-star Marko Polo Maradiso by Aminess, about 500 m from the old town, are accepted on request with charges set by hotel policy. Always get the fee in writing. Ground-floor units with a terrace or garden are far easier with a dog than upper floors in old-town houses.

## Best months and summer heat
July and August regularly reach 30–35 °C, and pavements and dark rock become too hot for paws by midday. Sea temperature reaches 25–28 °C. The best months are **May, June, September and early October**, when walking is comfortable, beaches are quieter, and there are fewer restrictions on busy sand. Never leave a dog in a parked car, and carry water and a collapsible bowl.

**Opinion:** The Split catamaran looks like the quickest way onto the island, but with a dog it is the worst choice. The deck cage fee can match a full adult fare, and rules vary by operator. Take a car ferry to Orebić or Vela Luka instead.

## Vet basics
Korčula has local veterinary services for routine matters, but the nearest 24-hour emergency clinic is on the mainland, with listings giving a distance of roughly 125 km. Save a vet's number before arrival and keep a printout of the pet passport. Ticks, sand flies (leishmaniasis risk in Dalmatia) and sea urchins are the usual hazards. Ask your home vet about tick and sand fly protection. Carry tweezers and a first-aid kit.

## EU pet passport rules for driving to Croatia
- **Microchip:** ISO microchip, implanted before the rabies vaccination.
- **Rabies vaccination:** At least 21 days before entry, and kept valid.
- **Documents:** EU pet passport or, for UK and non-EU travelers, an animal health certificate. Check current rules for your country before departure.
- **Limit:** Up to five pets per traveler for non-commercial travel.
- **Muzzles:** Croatian law requires muzzles for restricted breeds and on public transport, including ferries.
- **Transit:** Slovenia, Italy, Austria and Hungary follow the same EU rules, but drive with your documents at hand at every border.

## Verdict: how dog-friendly is Korčula?
Korčula is **moderately dog-friendly: 3.5 out of 5**. It has a named dog beach in Plitvine, relaxed old-town walking, many terraces that accept dogs and quiet coves for early swims. It loses points for the lack of official beaches near Korčula Town, the heat in midsummer, ferry restrictions and emergency vet distance. Come in May, June or September, travel by car ferry and book accommodation with a written dog policy.

faq.question: Is there a dog beach in Korčula?
faq.answer: Yes, Plitvine in Vela Luka is the named dog beach (plaža za pse). Other coves around Korčula Town, Lumbarda and Pelješac are used by dogs but are not officially designated, so check local signs.

faq.question: Are dogs allowed in Korčula Old Town?
faq.answer: Yes, leashed dogs can walk through the old town and along the waterfront. Terraces of many restaurants and cafés accept dogs, but indoor areas usually do not.

faq.question: Can dogs travel on ferries and catamarans to Korčula?
faq.answer: Yes, but rules vary. Jadrolinija carries dogs free on deck with a leash and muzzle, and dogs over 8 kg on catamarans use a pet box by request. Private catamarans such as Krilo charge 50–100% of the adult fare.

faq.question: How much do hotels and apartments charge for a dog in Korčula?
faq.answer: Typically about €5–€20 per night, sometimes with an extra cleaning fee. Confirm the fee and any size limit in writing before booking.

faq.question: What is the best month to visit Korčula with a dog?
faq.answer: May, June and September are best, with comfortable walking temperatures and quieter beaches. July and August often reach 30–35 °C, which is too hot for midday walks.

faq.question: What documents does a dog need to enter Croatia?
faq.answer: A microchip, a valid rabies vaccination given at least 21 days before travel, and an EU pet passport or animal health certificate. Up to five pets per traveler are allowed.

quickAnswer: Korčula is moderately dog-friendly. Leashed dogs can walk the old town and many pebble coves, and Plitvine near Vela Luka is the island's named dog beach. Ferries carry dogs on deck with a muzzle, accommodation usually adds a fee, and July–August heat is the main problem. May, June and September work best.
